name: ScyllaDB
use_cases: Real-time big data, IoT sensor data, ad-tech, time-series at scale
reasoning: ScyllaDB is a drop-in replacement for Apache Cassandra, rewritten in C++ for better performance. It uses the exact same wide-column data model with partition keys, clustering keys, and column families. It fits neatly into the Wide-Column family because it does not offer document, graph, or key-value abstractions beyond what Cassandra provides.

name: InfluxDB
use_cases: Infrastructure monitoring, IoT telemetry, real-time analytics, DevOps observability
reasoning: InfluxDB does NOT fit neatly into one traditional NoSQL family. Its primary identity is a purpose-built Time-Series database with a custom storage engine (TSM). However, its data model (measurements with tagged columns and timestamped fields) shares structural similarities with Wide-Column stores. It also supports SQL-like queries (InfluxQL / Flux), which is atypical for NoSQL. It is best classified as a specialized Time-Series store that borrows concepts from Wide-Column databases.

name: ArangoDB
data_model: JSON Documents with native graph traversal (AQL query language)
use_cases: Knowledge graphs, fraud detection, content management, recommendation engines
reasoning: ArangoDB explicitly does NOT fit into one NoSQL family. It is a true multi-model database that natively supports three data models in a single engine: (1) Document store (JSON/BSON-like), (2) Graph database (with native edge collections and traversals), and (3) Key-Value store. Unlike databases that bolt on graph support as an afterthought, ArangoDB was designed from the ground up to handle all three models with a unified query language (AQL). This makes it span Document, Graph, and Key-Value families simultaneously.
